questions.q: Which of these is a valid basic arithmetic calculated field in Tableau?
questions.explain: Tableau calculated fields use standard arithmetic operators directly on bracketed field names — Profit = [Sales] - [Cost] is exactly that.

questions.q: Why is Profit Ratio written as SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) rather than [Profit] / [Sales]?
options: The ratio needs to be calculated after aggregation, using total profit over total sales for whatever's on the view, not a row-by-row ratio
SUM() is required syntax for every calculated field, regardless of purpose
SUM() makes the formula run faster, with no effect on the result
questions.explain: Wrapping both sides in SUM() ensures the ratio is computed from aggregated totals (e.g., total profit over total sales for a region or category), which is what a KPI ratio should mean.

questions.q: Given Margin A = [Sales] - [Cost] / [Sales], what does Tableau compute first, and why?
options: [Cost] / [Sales], because division evaluates before subtraction unless parentheses say otherwise
The whole expression left to right regardless of operator
Tableau throws an error because the formula is ambiguous
questions.explain: Standard order of operations applies: division happens before subtraction, so [Cost] / [Sales] is computed first — likely not what was intended without parentheses.

questions.q: Which formula correctly computes profit margin as (Sales minus Cost), divided by Sales?
questions.explain: Parentheses around ([Sales] - [Cost]) force the subtraction to happen first, so the whole margin is then divided by Sales — exactly the intended calculation.

questions.q: Which of these best matches the 'index' KPI pattern described in the lesson?
options: Sales Index = SUM([Sales]) / [Target Sales] — comparing a total against a baseline or target
Profit Ratio = SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) — one total divided by another
Total Sales = SUM([Sales]) — a single aggregation with no comparison
questions.explain: An index compares a value against a baseline or target — Sales Index dividing total sales by a target is exactly that shape, distinct from the plain absolute and ratio patterns.
